DIABETES: A COMPREHENSIVE MEDICAL GUIDE

1. OVERVIEW
Diabetes mellitus is a chronic metabolic disease characterized by elevated levels of blood
glucose, which leads over time to serious damage to the heart, blood vessels, eyes, kidneys,
and nerves. There are three main types: Type 1, Type 2, and Gestational diabetes.
Globally, an estimated 422 million people have diabetes, and 1.5 million deaths are directly
attributed to the disease each year. The number of cases has been steadily rising over the
past few decades, particularly in low and middle income countries.

2. TYPES OF DIABETES
Type 1 Diabetes: An autoimmune condition in which the body's immune system attacks and
destroys insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. It requires daily insulin administration
and typically develops in children and young adults.

Type 2 Diabetes: The most common form, accounting for around 90% of all diabetes cases.
It occurs when the body does not use insulin effectively. It is strongly linked to obesity,
physical inactivity, and poor diet. It can often be managed through lifestyle changes.

Gestational Diabetes: A form of diabetes that develops during pregnancy and usually resolves
after delivery. However, it increases the risk of developing Type 2 diabetes later in life.

3. SYMPTOMS
Common symptoms of diabetes include:
- Frequent urination (polyuria)
- Excessive thirst (polydipsia)
- Unexplained weight loss
- Extreme fatigue and lack of energy
- Blurred vision
- Slow healing of wounds and cuts
- Tingling, numbness, or pain in hands and feet (neuropathy)
- Recurrent infections such as skin, gum, or bladder infections

Type 1 symptoms often appear suddenly, while Type 2 symptoms may develop gradually and
go unnoticed for years.

4. RISK FACTORS
The following factors increase the risk of developing Type 2 diabetes:
- Being overweight or obese with a BMI over 25
- Physical inactivity and sedentary lifestyle
- Family history of diabetes
- Age over 45 years
- High blood pressure (hypertension)
- History of gestational diabetes
- Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
- Unhealthy diet high in sugar and processed foods
- Smoking and excessive alcohol consumption
- Ethnicity with higher risk in African, Hispanic, Asian, and Indigenous populations

5. DIAGNOSIS
Diabetes is diagnosed through blood tests including:
- Fasting Blood Glucose Test: A reading of 126 mg/dL or higher after an 8-hour fast indicates diabetes.
- HbA1c Test: An HbA1c level of 6.5% or above confirms diabetes.
- Oral Glucose Tolerance Test: A 2-hour blood glucose of 200 mg/dL or higher indicates diabetes.
- Random Blood Sugar Test: A reading of 200 mg/dL or higher along with symptoms confirms diagnosis.

Pre-diabetes is diagnosed when blood glucose levels are higher than normal but not yet in the
diabetic range. Early detection is critical to preventing progression.

6. TREATMENT AND MANAGEMENT
Treatment depends on the type and severity of diabetes.

Medication: Type 1 diabetes requires insulin therapy. Type 2 diabetes may be managed with
oral medications such as Metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors, or GLP-1 receptor agonists.
Some Type 2 patients also require insulin.

Blood Sugar Monitoring: Regular self-monitoring using a glucometer helps patients track their
glucose levels and adjust treatment accordingly.

Diet: A balanced diet low in refined sugars, saturated fats, and processed foods is essential.
Emphasis should be placed on whole grains, vegetables, lean proteins, and healthy fats.

Exercise: At least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week is recommended.
Physical activity improves insulin sensitivity and helps maintain healthy body weight.

Regular Check-ups: Patients should have regular screenings for complications including eye exams,
kidney function tests, blood pressure monitoring, and foot examinations.

7. COMPLICATIONS
Uncontrolled diabetes can lead to serious complications:
- Cardiovascular disease: Heart attacks and strokes are 2 to 3 times more common in diabetic patients.
- Diabetic nephropathy: Kidney damage leading to chronic kidney disease or kidney failure.
- Diabetic retinopathy: Damage to blood vessels in the retina, a leading cause of blindness.
- Peripheral neuropathy: Nerve damage causing pain, numbness, and weakness in limbs.
- Diabetic foot: Poor circulation and neuropathy can lead to foot ulcers and in severe cases amputation.
- Increased susceptibility to infections due to weakened immune function.

8. PREVENTION
Type 2 diabetes can largely be prevented through lifestyle modifications:
- Maintain a healthy body weight through regular physical activity
- Follow a nutritious balanced diet rich in fibre and low in sugar
- Avoid smoking and limit alcohol consumption
- Get regular health screenings especially if you have risk factors
- Manage blood pressure and cholesterol levels
- Breastfeed infants when possible as it reduces diabetes risk in both mother and child

Public health interventions, community awareness, and early screening programs play a
critical role in reducing the global burden of diabetes.

9. GLOBAL STATISTICS
- 422 million people worldwide live with diabetes
- 1 in 10 adults globally has diabetes
- 1.5 million deaths are directly caused by diabetes annually
- Over 80% of diabetes deaths occur in low and middle income countries
- Type 2 diabetes accounts for approximately 90 to 95% of all diabetes cases
- Africa has the highest proportion of undiagnosed diabetes cases globally
- The global cost of diabetes related healthcare exceeds 760 billion dollars annually

10. WHEN TO SEE A DOCTOR
You should consult a healthcare professional if you experience:
- Persistent thirst or frequent urination
- Unexplained weight loss over a short period
- Fatigue that does not improve with rest
- Blurred vision or sudden changes in eyesight
- Slow healing wounds or recurring infections
- Numbness or tingling in your hands or feet

Early diagnosis and prompt treatment significantly reduce the risk of complications
and improve long-term quality of life.

MALARIA: A COMPREHENSIVE MEDICAL GUIDE

1. OVERVIEW
Malaria is a life-threatening disease caused by Plasmodium parasites transmitted to humans
through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. It is one of the most prevalent
infectious diseases in sub-Saharan Africa, accounting for over 90% of global malaria deaths.
Children under five and pregnant women are the most vulnerable groups.

2. TYPES OF MALARIA PARASITES
Plasmodium falciparum: The most deadly species, responsible for the majority of malaria
deaths in Africa. It can cause severe malaria and death within 24 hours if untreated.
Plasmodium vivax: Less deadly but capable of causing relapses months or years after
the initial infection due to dormant liver stages.
Plasmodium malariae: Causes a milder form of malaria but can persist in the blood
for decades if untreated.
Plasmodium ovale: Rare species found mainly in West Africa, similar to vivax in behavior.

3. SYMPTOMS
Early symptoms of malaria appear 10 to 15 days after the infective mosquito bite:
- Fever and chills (often cyclical, every 48 to 72 hours)
- Headache and body aches
- Nausea and vomiting
- Fatigue and weakness
- Sweating followed by a return to normal temperature

Severe malaria symptoms (Plasmodium falciparum):
- Extreme weakness or inability to sit, stand, or walk
- Impaired consciousness or coma (cerebral malaria)
- Seizures
- Respiratory distress and difficulty breathing
- Abnormal bleeding
- Jaundice (yellowing of skin and eyes)
- Dark or black urine (blackwater fever)

4. DIAGNOSIS
- Rapid Diagnostic Tests (RDTs): Detect malaria antigens in blood within 15 minutes.
  Widely available and used at community health level across Africa.
- Microscopy: Examination of blood smear under a microscope remains the gold standard
  for confirming species and parasite density.
- PCR Testing: Highly sensitive molecular test used in research settings.

5. TREATMENT
Uncomplicated malaria (Plasmodium falciparum):
- Artemisinin-based Combination Therapies (ACTs) are the WHO-recommended first-line treatment.
- Common ACTs include Artemether-Lumefantrine and Artesunate-Amodiaquine.
- Treatment course is typically 3 days.

Severe malaria:
- Intravenous or intramuscular Artesunate is the first-line treatment.
- Hospitalization is required for severe cases.
- Supportive care includes fluids, blood transfusion if needed, and seizure management.

Plasmodium vivax and ovale:
- Treated with Chloroquine plus Primaquine to eliminate liver-stage parasites.
- G6PD testing is required before Primaquine use as it can cause hemolysis in G6PD-deficient patients.

6. PREVENTION
- Insecticide-Treated Bed Nets (ITNs): Sleep under long-lasting insecticidal nets every night.
  This is the single most effective prevention measure in Africa.
- Indoor Residual Spraying (IRS): Spraying insecticide on walls and ceilings of homes kills
  mosquitoes that rest indoors.
- Chemoprevention: Seasonal Malaria Chemoprevention (SMC) for children in high-transmission areas.
  Intermittent Preventive Treatment in Pregnancy (IPTp) with Sulfadoxine-Pyrimethamine.
- Malaria Vaccine: The RTS,S/AS01 (Mosquirix) vaccine is recommended by WHO for children
  in moderate-to-high transmission areas. The R21/Matrix-M vaccine was approved in 2023.
- Environmental control: Eliminate standing water where mosquitoes breed.
- Wear long-sleeved clothing and use insect repellent during peak mosquito hours (dusk to dawn).

7. MALARIA IN PREGNANCY
Malaria in pregnancy increases risk of maternal anemia, low birth weight, and maternal death.
Pregnant women should:
- Sleep under insecticide-treated nets
- Receive IPTp starting from the second trimester
- Seek immediate treatment if fever develops

8. GLOBAL STATISTICS
- 249 million malaria cases were recorded globally in 2022 (WHO)
- Africa accounts for 94% of all malaria cases and 95% of malaria deaths
- Children under 5 account for 80% of all malaria deaths in Africa
- Nigeria, Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda, and Mozambique together account for
  over 50% of global malaria cases
- An estimated 608,000 people died from malaria in 2022

9. WHEN TO SEEK MEDICAL CARE
Seek immediate medical care if you experience:
- Fever above 38.5 degrees Celsius especially after travel to or residence in a malaria area
- Fever combined with chills, headache, and body aches
- Any symptoms of severe malaria listed above
- Fever in a child under five years in a malaria-endemic area
Malaria can become life-threatening within hours. Do not wait for symptoms to worsen.

HYPERTENSION (HIGH BLOOD PRESSURE): A COMPREHENSIVE MEDICAL GUIDE

1. OVERVIEW
Hypertension, commonly known as high blood pressure, is a chronic condition in which the
force of blood against artery walls is consistently too high. It is defined as a systolic
blood pressure of 140 mmHg or higher, or a diastolic blood pressure of 90 mmHg or higher.
Hypertension is called the silent killer because it typically has no symptoms but significantly
increases the risk of heart attack, stroke, kidney failure, and death.
In Africa, hypertension affects approximately 30% of adults and is the leading cause of
stroke and cardiovascular disease on the continent.

2. CLASSIFICATION OF BLOOD PRESSURE
- Normal: Systolic below 120 mmHg AND Diastolic below 80 mmHg
- Elevated: Systolic 120-129 mmHg AND Diastolic below 80 mmHg
- Stage 1 Hypertension: Systolic 130-139 mmHg OR Diastolic 80-89 mmHg
- Stage 2 Hypertension: Systolic 140 mmHg or higher OR Diastolic 90 mmHg or higher
- Hypertensive Crisis: Systolic above 180 mmHg OR Diastolic above 120 mmHg (requires emergency care)

3. SYMPTOMS
Hypertension is mostly asymptomatic. When symptoms occur they may include:
- Severe headaches (especially at the back of the head in the morning)
- Nosebleeds
- Shortness of breath
- Blurred or double vision
- Chest pain or palpitations
- Dizziness or lightheadedness
These symptoms usually only appear when blood pressure reaches dangerously high levels.

4. RISK FACTORS
Non-modifiable risk factors:
- Age: Risk increases significantly after age 45 in men and 65 in women
- Family history of hypertension
- Ethnicity: People of African descent have higher rates of hypertension and more severe forms

Modifiable risk factors:
- Obesity or overweight (BMI above 25)
- Physical inactivity
- High salt diet (sodium intake above 5 grams per day)
- Excessive alcohol consumption
- Smoking
- Chronic stress
- Diabetes
- Chronic kidney disease

5. DIAGNOSIS
Blood pressure is measured using a sphygmomanometer or digital blood pressure monitor.
Diagnosis requires:
- Two or more elevated readings taken on two or more separate visits
- Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (24-hour monitoring) for confirmation
- Home blood pressure monitoring for ongoing management

6. TREATMENT AND MANAGEMENT
Lifestyle modifications (first line for Stage 1):
- Reduce salt intake to less than 5 grams per day
- Follow the DASH diet (rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, low-fat dairy)
- Exercise at least 150 minutes of moderate activity per week
- Achieve and maintain a healthy body weight
- Limit alcohol to no more than 1-2 drinks per day
- Stop smoking
- Manage stress through relaxation techniques

Medications (for Stage 2 or if lifestyle changes are insufficient):
- ACE Inhibitors (e.g. Lisinopril, Enalapril): Relax blood vessels
- ARBs (e.g. Losartan, Valsartan): Block angiotensin to lower blood pressure
- Calcium Channel Blockers (e.g. Amlodipine, Nifedipine): Relax and widen blood vessels
- Diuretics (e.g. Hydrochlorothiazide, Furosemide): Reduce fluid volume
- Beta-Blockers (e.g. Atenolol, Metoprolol): Slow heart rate
Most patients in Africa require two or more medications for adequate blood pressure control.

7. COMPLICATIONS OF UNCONTROLLED HYPERTENSION
- Stroke: Hypertension is the single most important risk factor for stroke in Africa
- Heart attack and heart failure
- Kidney damage and chronic kidney disease
- Retinopathy (damage to blood vessels in the eye, leading to vision loss)
- Peripheral artery disease
- Aortic aneurysm

8. HYPERTENSION IN AFRICA
- Hypertension affects an estimated 130 million adults in sub-Saharan Africa
- Awareness rates are low: fewer than 40% of people with hypertension in Africa know they have it
- Treatment rates are even lower: fewer than 10% achieve controlled blood pressure
- Factors include limited access to healthcare, cost of medications, and low health literacy
- Salt intake in many African countries far exceeds WHO recommended limits

- Regular blood pressure screening from age 18 onward, or earlier with risk factors
- Reduce dietary salt by avoiding processed foods, seasoning cubes, and adding less salt
- Maintain a healthy weight through diet and physical activity
- Avoid excessive alcohol consumption
- Manage stress
- Do not smoke

10. WHEN TO SEE A DOCTOR
- Blood pressure reading above 140/90 mmHg on two separate occasions
- Sudden severe headache, chest pain, or shortness of breath with high blood pressure
  (this is a hypertensive crisis requiring emergency care)
- Any symptoms of stroke: sudden face drooping, arm weakness, speech difficulty

TUBERCULOSIS (TB): A COMPREHENSIVE MEDICAL GUIDE

1. OVERVIEW
Tuberculosis (TB) is an infectious disease caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
It primarily affects the lungs (pulmonary TB) but can affect any organ in the body
(extrapulmonary TB). TB spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes,
or speaks. Africa carries approximately 25% of the global TB burden, with Nigeria, South Africa,
and the Democratic Republic of Congo among the highest-burden countries.

2. TYPES OF TUBERCULOSIS
Latent TB: The bacteria are present in the body but inactive. The person has no symptoms
and cannot spread TB. However, latent TB can become active if the immune system weakens.
Active TB: The bacteria are active and causing illness. The person is infectious and can
spread TB to others.
Pulmonary TB: Affects the lungs. The most common form and the most contagious.
Extrapulmonary TB: Affects organs other than the lungs including lymph nodes, bones,
kidneys, brain (TB meningitis), and the lining around the heart (TB pericarditis).
Drug-Resistant TB: Caused by bacteria that are resistant to standard TB drugs.
Multi-Drug Resistant TB (MDR-TB) is resistant to Isoniazid and Rifampicin.

3. SYMPTOMS
Pulmonary TB symptoms:
- Persistent cough lasting 2 weeks or more (often with blood-stained sputum)
- Chest pain and difficulty breathing
- Fever, especially in the evenings
- Night sweats
- Unexplained weight loss and loss of appetite
- Extreme fatigue and weakness

Extrapulmonary TB symptoms vary depending on the organ affected:
- TB lymphadenitis: Swollen lymph nodes in the neck
- TB meningitis: Severe headache, stiff neck, confusion
- TB pericarditis: Chest pain, shortness of breath, swelling of legs
- Skeletal TB: Back pain, joint swelling

4. RISK FACTORS
- HIV infection: People living with HIV are 18 times more likely to develop active TB
- Close contact with someone with active TB
- Living in overcrowded or poorly ventilated conditions
- Malnutrition and poverty
- Diabetes mellitus
- Smoking
- Excessive alcohol use
- Immunosuppressive medications (e.g. corticosteroids, biologics)
- Age: Young children and elderly adults are more vulnerable

5. DIAGNOSIS
- Sputum Smear Microscopy: Examines sputum (mucus from lungs) under a microscope for
  TB bacteria. Quick and widely available in Africa.
- GeneXpert (Xpert MTB/RIF): A molecular test that detects TB DNA and rifampicin resistance
  within 2 hours. WHO-recommended and increasingly available in Africa.
- Tuberculin Skin Test (TST/Mantoux): Tests for immune response to TB. Cannot distinguish
  latent from active TB.
- Chest X-ray: Shows characteristic patterns of TB in the lungs.
- Culture: Growing the bacteria in the laboratory. Most sensitive test but takes 4-6 weeks.

6. TREATMENT
Standard treatment for drug-susceptible TB (6-month course):
- Intensive Phase (2 months): Isoniazid + Rifampicin + Pyrazinamide + Ethambutol
- Continuation Phase (4 months): Isoniazid + Rifampicin
Treatment is provided free of charge in most African countries through national TB programs.

Drug-Resistant TB treatment:
- MDR-TB requires 9-18 months of treatment with second-line drugs including Bedaquiline,
  Linezolid, and Levofloxacin.
- Treatment is more toxic and more expensive than standard TB treatment.

Important notes on treatment:
- All doses must be taken as prescribed without missing any doses
- Stopping treatment early is the main cause of drug resistance
- Directly Observed Therapy (DOT) involves a healthcare worker watching the patient take
  each dose to ensure adherence

7. TB AND HIV CO-INFECTION
- Sub-Saharan Africa has the highest burden of TB-HIV co-infection globally
- All TB patients should be tested for HIV and all HIV patients should be screened for TB
- People living with HIV on antiretroviral therapy (ART) have a significantly lower risk
  of developing active TB
- TB is the leading cause of death among people living with HIV in Africa

8. PREVENTION
- BCG Vaccination: Given to newborns in most African countries, provides protection

- TB Preventive Therapy (TPT): Isoniazid for 6 months or Rifapentine + Isoniazid weekly
  for 12 weeks, given to people with latent TB or high risk groups including those with HIV
- Improve ventilation in homes, schools, and healthcare facilities
- Early diagnosis and treatment of active TB cases to prevent spread
- Address social determinants: poverty, malnutrition, and overcrowding

9. GLOBAL STATISTICS
- 10.6 million people fell ill with TB globally in 2022 (WHO)
- 1.3 million people died from TB in 2022, making it the second leading infectious killer
  after COVID-19
- Africa accounts for 23% of all TB cases and 31% of TB deaths globally
- Nigeria, South Africa, and DR Congo are among the 30 high-burden TB countries

10. WHEN TO SEEK MEDICAL CARE
- Cough lasting 2 weeks or more, especially with blood in sputum
- Unexplained weight loss combined with fever and night sweats
- Known close contact with a TB patient
- HIV-positive individuals should be screened for TB at every healthcare visit

MATERNAL HEALTH: A COMPREHENSIVE MEDICAL GUIDE

1. OVERVIEW
Maternal health refers to the health of women during pregnancy, childbirth, and the
postnatal period. Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for approximately 70% of global maternal
deaths despite having only 15% of the world's population. The majority of these deaths
are preventable with skilled care and access to essential services.
The maternal mortality ratio in sub-Saharan Africa is approximately 545 deaths per 100,000
live births, compared to a global average of 223 per 100,000 live births.

2. ANTENATAL CARE (CARE DURING PREGNANCY)
WHO recommends at least 8 antenatal care (ANC) contacts during pregnancy:
- First contact before 12 weeks of pregnancy
- Additional contacts at 20, 26, 30, 34, 36, 38, and 40 weeks

Key components of antenatal care:
- Blood pressure monitoring to detect pre-eclampsia and hypertension
- Blood tests for anemia, blood group, HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B
- Urine testing for protein (signs of pre-eclampsia) and infection
- Ultrasound scanning to confirm gestational age and fetal position
- Nutritional supplementation: Iron, folic acid, and calcium
- Malaria prevention: Insecticide-treated nets and intermittent preventive treatment (IPTp)
- Tetanus vaccination to protect mother and newborn
- Birth planning and emergency preparedness

3. DANGER SIGNS DURING PREGNANCY
Seek immediate medical attention if you experience:
- Severe headache with visual disturbances (signs of pre-eclampsia)
- Swelling of face, hands, and legs (oedema)
- Vaginal bleeding at any stage of pregnancy
- Reduced or absent fetal movements after 28 weeks
- High fever
- Severe abdominal pain
- Water breaking before labor begins (premature rupture of membranes)
- Difficulty breathing

4. MAJOR CAUSES OF MATERNAL DEATH IN AFRICA
- Haemorrhage (excessive bleeding): Accounts for 27% of maternal deaths.
  Can occur before delivery (antepartum) or after delivery (postpartum haemorrhage, PPH)
- Hypertensive disorders (pre-eclampsia and eclampsia): 14% of maternal deaths
- Infections and sepsis: 11% of maternal deaths
- Unsafe abortion complications: 8% of maternal deaths
- Obstructed labor: Prolonged labor where the baby cannot descend through the birth canal
- Anaemia: Severe anaemia during pregnancy increases the risk of death from haemorrhage

5. PRE-ECLAMPSIA AND ECLAMPSIA
Pre-eclampsia is high blood pressure (above 140/90 mmHg) after 20 weeks of pregnancy
combined with protein in the urine.
Eclampsia is pre-eclampsia that progresses to seizures and is life-threatening.
Warning signs:
- Severe headache
- Blurred vision or seeing flashing lights
- Severe swelling of face and hands
- Upper abdominal pain
- Sudden weight gain

Treatment includes:
- Magnesium sulphate to prevent and treat seizures
- Antihypertensive medications to control blood pressure
- Delivery of the baby as soon as the mother is stabilized

6. POSTNATAL CARE (CARE AFTER DELIVERY)
The first 24 hours after delivery are the most critical for both mother and baby.
Postnatal care contacts are recommended at:
- Within 24 hours of delivery
- 3 days after delivery
- 1 to 2 weeks after delivery
- 6 weeks after delivery

Monitoring for:
- Postpartum haemorrhage (the leading cause of maternal death)
- Signs of infection including fever, foul-smelling vaginal discharge
- Mental health: postpartum depression affects 1 in 5 women in Africa
- Breastfeeding support and family planning counselling

7. SKILLED BIRTH ATTENDANCE
- All deliveries should be attended by a skilled health professional (doctor, nurse, or midwife)
- In sub-Saharan Africa, only 59% of births are attended by skilled health personnel
- Facility-based deliveries have significantly lower maternal and newborn mortality rates
- Traditional birth attendants should be integrated into the referral system

8. FAMILY PLANNING
- Spacing pregnancies by at least 2 years reduces maternal and child mortality
- Modern contraception methods include hormonal methods (pills, injectables, implants),
  barrier methods (condoms), intrauterine devices (IUDs), and permanent methods
- Unintended pregnancy rates in Africa remain among the highest globally
- Family planning also reduces unsafe abortions

9. MATERNAL NUTRITION
- Iron and folic acid supplementation should begin as early as possible in pregnancy
- Calcium supplementation reduces the risk of pre-eclampsia
- A balanced diet including protein, fruits, vegetables, and whole grains is essential
- Avoid alcohol, tobacco, and traditional herbal remedies during pregnancy

10. WHEN TO SEEK MEDICAL CARE DURING PREGNANCY AND POSTPARTUM
During pregnancy:
- At the first sign of pregnancy for early antenatal care registration
- Any of the danger signs listed in section 3 above
After delivery:
- Heavy bleeding soaking more than one pad per hour
- High fever above 38 degrees Celsius
- Severe abdominal pain
- Signs of postpartum depression including persistent sadness, inability to care for baby

TYPHOID FEVER: A COMPREHENSIVE MEDICAL GUIDE

1. OVERVIEW
Typhoid fever is a serious bacterial infection caused by Salmonella typhi. It spreads
through contaminated food and water. Typhoid is endemic across West Africa, including
Nigeria, where inadequate water supply and sanitation create widespread transmission.
An estimated 11 to 21 million cases of typhoid fever occur globally each year, causing
128,000 to 161,000 deaths. The burden is highest in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa.

2. HOW IT SPREADS
Typhoid spreads through the fecal-oral route:
- Drinking water contaminated with Salmonella typhi from infected human waste
- Eating food handled by an infected person who did not wash their hands
- Eating raw fruits and vegetables washed with contaminated water
- Eating shellfish from contaminated water sources
Carriers: Some people carry the bacteria without showing symptoms and can spread it to others.

3. SYMPTOMS
Typhoid fever develops gradually over 1 to 3 weeks after exposure:

Week 1:
- Gradually rising fever reaching 39 to 40 degrees Celsius
- Headache
- General weakness and fatigue
- Dry cough
- Abdominal discomfort

Week 2:
- Sustained high fever
- Slow heartbeat (relative bradycardia) despite high fever
- Rose spots: small, flat pink spots appearing on the abdomen and chest
- Enlarged spleen and liver
- Abdominal distension and pain
- Diarrhoea (sometimes constipation in adults)

Week 3 (if untreated):
- Serious complications including intestinal perforation
- Peritonitis (infection of the abdominal cavity)
- Severe bleeding
- Altered mental status, delirium (typhoid state)

4. DIAGNOSIS
- Blood Culture: The gold standard for diagnosis. Detects Salmonella typhi in the blood.
  Most effective in the first week of illness.
- Widal Test: Measures antibodies against Salmonella. Widely used in Africa but has
  significant false positives and negatives and should not be used alone for diagnosis.
- Typhidot Test and Tubex Test: Rapid serological tests increasingly used in Africa.
- Bone Marrow Culture: The most sensitive test but rarely needed in routine practice.
- Stool and Urine Culture: Useful in later stages of illness.

5. TREATMENT
Antibiotic therapy is the cornerstone of treatment:
- Fluoroquinolones (e.g. Ciprofloxacin): Previously the first-line treatment but resistance
  is now widespread in Africa and Asia.
- Third-generation Cephalosporins (e.g. Ceftriaxone, Cefixime): Current first-line treatment
  in most African settings due to fluoroquinolone resistance.
- Azithromycin: Effective for uncomplicated typhoid, especially in areas with quinolone resistance.
- Supportive care: Adequate fluid intake, fever management with paracetamol, rest,
  and nutritional support.

Drug-resistant typhoid:
- Extensively Drug-Resistant (XDR) typhoid is resistant to multiple antibiotics including
  fluoroquinolones and is emerging as a major concern.
- Azithromycin remains effective for most XDR typhoid cases.

Surgical treatment may be required for:
- Intestinal perforation (a surgical emergency)
- Severe intestinal bleeding

6. COMPLICATIONS
If typhoid is untreated or inadequately treated:
- Intestinal perforation: Occurs in up to 3% of cases. Life-threatening surgical emergency.
- Intestinal bleeding
- Encephalopathy (brain dysfunction)
- Myocarditis (heart muscle inflammation)
- Pneumonia
- Relapse: Occurs in 5 to 10% of patients after completing antibiotic treatment

7. PREVENTION
- Safe water: Drink only boiled, filtered, or bottled water. Avoid ice made from tap water.
- Food safety: Eat only thoroughly cooked food served hot. Avoid raw vegetables, salads,
  and street food in high-risk areas.
- Hand hygiene: Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water before eating and after using
  the toilet. This is the single most important prevention measure.
- Sanitation: Proper sewage disposal and sanitation infrastructure to prevent water contamination.
- Typhoid vaccination: Two vaccines are available:
  Vi polysaccharide vaccine (Typhim Vi): Single injection, protective for 2-3 years.
  Ty21a oral vaccine: 3-4 capsules taken orally on alternate days.

8. TYPHOID IN NIGERIA AND WEST AFRICA
- Nigeria has one of the highest typhoid burdens in Africa due to contaminated water supply
  and inadequate sanitation affecting over 60% of the population
- Self-medication with antibiotics is common and contributes to drug resistance
- The Widal test is overused and leads to misdiagnosis and overtreatment
- WHO recommends introduction of Typhoid Conjugate Vaccine (TCV) into routine immunization

9. WHEN TO SEEK MEDICAL CARE
- Fever lasting more than 3 days especially combined with headache and abdominal pain
- Rose spots on the abdomen
- Severe abdominal pain (may indicate perforation)
- Signs of delirium or altered consciousness
- Return of fever after appearing to improve (may indicate relapse or complication)
Do not self-medicate with antibiotics without proper diagnosis as this masks symptoms
and contributes to drug resistance.
